title: Brief Drafting with Machine Assistance
answer: Brief drafting with machine assistance covers the use of AI tools to produce, structure, and revise legal briefs, memoranda, and motions. It spans research summarisation, argument outlining, citation checking, and first-draft prose, while the lawyer retains authorship and sign-off. The work sits inside legal research and case strategy, where the brief is the main written product of a case. It is distinct from fully automated filing, since a human lawyer reviews and adopts every word.

sections.body: Brief drafting with machine assistance covers the use of AI tools to produce, structure, and revise legal briefs, memoranda, and motions. It spans research summarisation, argument outlining, citation checking, and first-draft prose, while the lawyer retains authorship and sign-off. The work sits inside legal research and case strategy, where the brief is the main written product of a case. It is distinct from fully automated filing, since a human lawyer reviews and adopts every word.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: These tools run on large language models accessed through legal research platforms or general chat interfaces, often paired with firm document management systems and citators. Some products are trained or tuned on case law and statutes, while others rely on general models with retrieval over a firm's own precedent bank. Output is typically produced in a word processor or drafting environment, then checked against primary sources.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A typical workflow starts with a lawyer supplying facts, issues, and jurisdiction, then asking the tool for an outline, a summary of authorities, or a draft section. The lawyer verifies every citation against the original source, because models can generate plausible but nonexistent cases. Drafts are then edited for tone, accuracy, and argument, and the final brief is filed under the lawyer's name. Some teams keep a record of prompts and model versions to show how a draft was produced.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Professional conduct rules on competence, supervision, confidentiality, and candour apply to machine-assisted drafting just as they do to any other work product. Courts in several jurisdictions now require disclosure when AI is used in preparing a filing, and sanctions have followed fabricated citations. Client material fed into a third-party model may raise privilege and data protection questions, so firms often restrict which tools can see which documents. The site tracks 29 AI case law precedents and 152 active AI lawsuits, 92 of them intellectual property, as the surrounding body of authority grows.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Expect tighter integration between drafting tools and verified case law databases, so citations are checked at the point of generation rather than after. Courts and bar bodies are likely to keep refining disclosure expectations, and model providers will keep adding audit trails. The practical effect is that drafting speed rises while review discipline becomes the binding constraint.
